name: Athabaskan-Eyak
defining_innovation: The common ancestor of Eyak and the Athabaskan languages, whose close relationship Michael Krauss demonstrated in the 1960s.

chapters.title: Eyak's Relatives
chapters.body: Until the 1930s Eyak was hardly known. The anthropologist Frederica de Laguna recorded it, and in the 1960s **Michael Krauss** showed that it is the sister of the whole Athabaskan branch. It shares with Athabaskan the verb structure and the regular correspondences that allow Proto-Athabaskan-Eyak to be reconstructed, but it stands apart from all the Athabaskan languages in its vocabulary and sounds.

chapters.title: Rebuilding the Common Ancestor
chapters.body:
Krauss set out the case in two papers, 'Proto-Athapaskan-Eyak and the Problem of Na-Dene', published in the *International Journal of American Linguistics* in 1964 and 1965. His method was the standard comparative one, but applied to a verb built almost entirely of prefixes. He matched Eyak's prefixes with Athabaskan ones slot by slot, including the 'classifier' prefixes that change a verb's voice, and then showed that the consonants of the stems corresponded regularly, series by series, including Athabaskan's several sets of affricates.

The result was important in two ways. It gave Proto-Athabaskan a sister, so that features found in both Eyak and Athabaskan could be pushed back one stage further, to Proto-Athabaskan-Eyak. And it gave a firmer base for comparison with Tlingit, which is much further away: Leer's later correspondences between Tlingit and the rest were worked out against the reconstructed Athabaskan-Eyak forms rather than against any single modern language.

Eyak on its own is only a partial witness, because it was documented late and from few speakers. Much of what can be said about Proto-Athabaskan-Eyak therefore rests on the careful records Krauss made in the 1960s and 1970s.

speakers.note: Almost all are Navajo speakers; US census figures count people who speak a language at home, which is not quite the same as first-language speakers.

turning_points.title: Eyak and Athabaskan part
turning_points.description: The ancestors of Eyak settle on the south Alaskan coast, while those of the Athabaskans remain in the interior. The date is a rough estimate.
